text: This is Nerve. It watches a simulated device fleet. Most monitors show a red graph and stop. You build the theory yourself.
Every tool in this category does this part. Filter, sort, stare. The staring is where your shift goes.
Nerve groups the alerts first. Fifteen of them shared a site or a metric. They collapsed into five readable incidents, each naming its own site and why it grouped.

Here is the theory. Three mills at Osaka, all past four sigma on vibration. One shared cause beats three separate faults. The hypothesis carries its own evidence, a runbook, and one command that goes to every affected machine, audit logged. Confidence is printed. The badge says deterministic, because no model wrote this one.
This is the layer underneath. Every alert carries its own device baseline, so the threshold was learned, not typed in.

Now the machine itself. Every metric from raw readings, against the operating range its type declares. Counters, state and open alerts sit beside the charts. This is where you confirm a theory, not where you form one.

Ask in plain English. The answer never comes from a model. A plan does. Xano validates every field against an allowlist, then runs it. Today the model was unreachable, so the fallback wrote the plan. Every question is logged with its plan and its latency.

text: Rules are written as sentences. Critical if this machine vibrates three sigma above its own baseline. The table reads each rule back the same way, with its fire count beside it.
Keys, schemas, an audit log. The whole backend is XanoScript. And the graph was never the hard part.
